title: Art Discipline .28
subtitle: The Friction to Take Off
excerpt: I have always overworked in order to keep improving and keep my art path going forward.
body:
I have always overworked in order to keep improving and keep my art path going forward.

At the beginning of my career, in order to get my first jobs, I worked as much as possible to the extreme.

I believe this is necessary for anyone to learn quickly, stand out as an artist, and accomplish your goals.

Trying to demonstrate you can actually do the job before anyone hires you is fucking hard. The friction to take off requires the most fuel.

But after you achieve something where you’re happy, it would make sense to stop the overwork and balance life.

The issue is that the inertia is hard to stop.

It took me a few years making games and visual development full-time, doing a shit ton of extra work on my own without a proper goal, before I realised I needed to stop a bit and actually live life.

I wasn’t completely hiding in a cave, but I was saying no to too many things and not actually having fun at all.

I didn’t see fun as productive.

Next time, I’ll share how breaking that inertia completely changed the way I look at my work.

Stay creative, stay weird <3

title: Art Discipline .26
subtitle: Ego vs Learning: Clash of Clans
excerpt: Not long ago I thought my career in games was in decline. It might sound exaggerated, but after OlliOlli World, I convinced myself I couldn’t do better, whatever that means.
body:
Not long ago I thought my career in games was in decline. It might sound exaggerated, but after OlliOlli World, I convinced myself I couldn’t do better, whatever that means.

Fast forward to today, and I can honestly say I am experiencing one of the best periods of my professional life.
(Artistically blocked like mentioned in the last drop tho hahah)

A big part of it has been going back into apprentice mode.

Ego vs Learning_

For almost two years, I’ve been working as an artist on Clash of Clans, Supercell. Right before starting, I was meditating on my career, unsure of what direction to take or which path was right for me.

Then this opportunity to work on Clash came along.

During one of my first meetings with team members they asked me if I would be interested in learning Blender to be more of a generalist artists (one of the requirements to be in the art team).

It had been some time since I learned a new technique. I was curious about what I could do on my own work using 3D, I liked the project and company, so I said yes.

Still, part of my ego was questioning why I needed to learn something new for work.

For a few years, I had been working with studios that approached me specifically for art direction and creative input based on my existing work.

I realized I was too comfortable with my art skills, and that refusing to learn something new just to keep repeating a familiar pattern was my ego getting in the way of improving.

In the right dose, ego is a good thing. But when it’s unbalanced, it creates a major issue, stagnation.

If you already think you're good enough, why bother improving?

Apprentice Mode_

In the months before Clash came along, I had been taking some time to draw, read, and reflect on these exact subjects.

When the offer arrived, I realized it meant working on a project with a larger scale than anything I had ever experienced. The team is full of incredible professionals, and I was going to have to learn new techniques, new processes, and adapt to an existing IP (when I started, it was a 12 year old game with a massive amount of existing content).

The perfect combination to forget about ego or being comfortable.

Ego_

I found my mission again: learning 3D from scratch, understanding the IP, and improving my design skills for a game with high standards.

Having an ego is not a bad thing, we need it in balance.

But a high ego and a learning mindset are simply not compatible.

Ego creates a barrier, stopping new knowledge from getting through.

And that’s a trap because it hurts you in the long term. In the moment you may feel good but it blocks you from listening to whom is trying to teach you.

Keep the apprentice mode on, and you’ll be surprised by the things that come your way.

Stay creative, stay weird <3

title: Art Discipline .25
subtitle: Lost
excerpt: Art Discipline is my creative journal, for the good and the bad stuff. It just makes sense that I share something from my current situation when I feel it’s important.
body:
Art Discipline is my creative journal, for the good and the bad stuff. It just makes sense that I share something from my current situation when I feel it’s important.

Sometimes I share general ideas and concepts from art making, or just projects I have worked on.

By now I thought I would have more stuff figured out art wise and on creating projects.

I’m at the most successful point of my career professionally,

and

I don’t think I have ever been this lost with my direction as an artist.

I wanted to be a concept artist in games, made it.

Then I wanted to set the art direction for games and different projects. Made it as well (with some caveats I will explain in the future).

But what about my own art? I feel trapped in the way I work and I am unhappy about it for some reason.

That’s why I am not drawing more than what I strictly need to.

Over time I have been trying to check boxes rather than having fun with my own art.

Everything I started had a clear purpose and goal in the big picture of my career. But I forgot to do something just for the sake of doing it and having fun.

I’ve arrived at this conclusion and now I don’t know what to do.

Any direction is a possible path. I don’t take any because that means not taking the others.

That’s so stupid.

I could just not share this and act like a cool artist that got everything figured out. But that’s not the case.

I’m happy with my career in games, made it to places I would never have thought I could work.

But

I feel less of an artist than ever

and

I will openly share here what I try to do.

Stay creative <3

title: Art Discipline .24
subtitle: Intention in Practice
excerpt: Hey there, Germán here 🌞!
body:
Hey there, Germán here 🌞!

Skipping steps can be a time saver or a learning killer. It all depends on the context.

As an artist in the games industry, most of the time you’re looking for visual solutions, not just pretty final images. That means embracing what most people consider “cheating” in order to achieve a good solution quickly.

But as an artist trying to arrive at a beautiful and interesting piece, the process is important.

The How_

The how comes first, then the what.

In commercial production, the how doesn’t matter as much. This is a key difference between independent work and working for companies.

In my own work, the how translates into a deliberate process of thinking how I express ideas.

In Megalith, the graphic novel I’m developing with Lizz Lunney, I do something that may seem inefficient in terms of time. But I think it helps me achieve the visual quality I’m looking for in order to tell the story.

Intention in Storytelling_

For me, that means reading the script from Lizz and storyboarding on paper. In the same format I would do for animation in frames:

This part is the most creatively important to me because I think about the flow of how we are telling the scenes, the pacing, and the visual metaphors.

I’m not thinking on page layouts or panel shapes yet; it is purely cinematic thinking.

The next step is making the rough pages in Photoshop just because it is more flexible to me.

I take the script + storyboard, and I start thinking on the page layout, revisiting the pacing of the scene and making any changes or additions.

Problem Solving_

This process means I am practically drawing two storyboards.

This way, I separate the problem-solving into two steps:

  1. Initial shots and visuals for the scenes.

  2. Page composition.


It also gives me room to double-check things throughout this two step process.

After the roughs, I check with Lizz to see if she has any notes. Once that is done, cleaning up the lines means thinking purely about the design of all the elements, poses of the characters, perspective, etc.

Basically polishing the drawing.

You can read Megalith pages and support us in Patreon!

Intention_

This entire process gives me intention. It gives me the space to take care of the different elements of every page, ensuring the visuals are tied closely to the script while expanding the story through the art.

There’s no “wasted time” here. You just need care and intention in your process.

The goal is to tell you a story we believe in, not to achieve some metrics.

Stay creative, stay weird <3

excerpt: “An old man in Calcutta walk to get water from a well everyday. He’d carry a clay of pot and lower it by hand slowly, all the way down, careful not to let it hit the sides of the well and break.
body:
“An old man in Calcutta walk to get water from a well everyday. He’d carry a clay of pot and lower it by hand slowly, all the way down, careful not to let it hit the sides of the well and break.

Once it was full, he’d raise the pot slowly and carefully again. It was a focused, time-consuming act.

One day, a traveler noticed the old man engaged in this dificult task. More experienced with mechanics, he showed the old man how to use a pulley system.

“This will allow the pot to go straight down quickly,” the traveler explained, “then fill with water and come back up, without hitting the sides. It’s much easier and the pot will be just as full with much less work.”

The old man looked at him and said, “I think I’m going to keep doing it the way I always have. I really have to think about each movement and there’s a great deal of care that goes into doing it right. I’d imagine if I were to use the pulley, it would become easy and I might even start thinking about something else while doing it. If I put so little care and time into it, what might the water taste like? It couldn’t possibly taste as good.”

From The Creative Act by Rick Rubins

I keep thinking about this story each time someone tells me to hire someone to do certain parts of my work as if that was a natural part of growing, or just to use AI.

This is why a project like Megalith feels so important to me right now.

Intention, time, effort, failing, learning, using your own brain.

Reading Lizz’s scripts carefully, storyboarding on paper:

Working on each page as if it was an illustration.

No “efficiency”, no ROI, no bullshit.

Stay Weird,

<3

title: Art Discipline .22
subtitle: 3 Rules of The Creative Act(ing)
excerpt: We see many people online talking about business, entrepreneurship and so on.
body:
We see many people online talking about business, entrepreneurship and so on.

It’s easier to talk about money and data because they can be easily measured.

But few share the struggles along a creative path.

Of course, we all need money to survive, but focusing purely on art comes with its own unique struggles and requires specific mental tools to succeed.

In my career, I found a way to work as an artist in game production to earn an income. Naturally, you have to make some creative compromises to achieve this.

My strategy has always been to do this, while releasing the pressure of my creative interests on the side.

Right now, this is Megalith, the project that Lizz and I are developing out of love to tell a story and create a beautiful book.

In this new drop, you will find 3 rules of the creative path.

(If you need guidance in your own art journey: art for games, animation, comic books, illustration, etc.

I’ve opened slots for my mentorship 1:1 sessions.

Adapted to your needs, available here)

Rick Rubin’s bathroom book_

He is quite a character, almost putting on an act, and the title of his book suits him perfectly.

But I don’t think it’s a bad read.

You just have to take it with a grain of salt; depending on your current situation, you will interpret it differently.

This book served as a great reminder of certain aspects of art-making, while also offering some fresh perspectives on the creative process.

These are perspectives you might have blocked out because you were too focused on doing things a 'certain way,' or because you were taught your craft through a narrow lens.

Here are 3 rules of the creative path with quotes from The Creative Act by Rick Rubin.

1_Everyone is a creator_

“Creativity doesn’t exclusively relate to making art. We all engage in this act on a daily basis. To create is to bring something into existence that wasn’t there before.

As artist we seek to restore our childlike perception:

A more innocent state of wonder and appreciation not tethered to utility or survival.”

This is something I am applying to my personal projects. The ones that don’t need to have a financial return.

Explore and share purely using your voice and taste.

2_Self-Doubt_

“Flaws human, and the attraction of art is the humanity held in it.

Yes, you may need to deepen your craft to fully realize your vision. If you’re not up to it, no one else can do it. Only you can. You’re the only one with your voice.

If a creator is so afraid of judgement that they’re unable to move forward, it might be that the desire to share the work isn’t as strong as the desire to protect themselves.”

We all have something special. Our tastes and interests, filtered through our own experiences, create something entirely unique.

Don’t follow what others do or try to replicate them. If you do, you'll become a copy of something else, a path doomed to failure.

Ironically, taking the risk to put yourself out there actually increases your chances of success.

3_Rules_

“Rules direct us to average behaviours. If we’re aiming to create works that are exceptional, most rules don’t apply. Average is nothing to aspire to.

The goal is not to fit in. If anything, it’s to amplify the differences, what doesn’t fit, the special characteristics unique to how you see the world.

Instead of sounding lie others, value your own voice.

In the beginning, we approach our craft with a template of what’s come before.

The templates of the past can be an inspiration in the beginning phases, but it’s helpful to think beyond what’s been done before. The world isn’t waiting for more of the same.

Often, the most innovative ideas come from those who master the rules to such a degree that they can see past them or from those who never learned them at all.”

We all start by learning the rules, which naturally pushes us toward the average. But excellence comes from breaking these rules and exploring.

Sticking rigidly to the rules is a sure path to failure, not just for your career, but for yourself.

What We Tell Ourselves_

“All our efforts to make sense of ourselves and our art are a smoke screen, an obfuscation. They don’t illuminate what is. They mislead us.

We tell ourselves varying stories of who we are and how the works gets made. But none of them matter.

With each story we tell ourselves, we negate possibility. Reality is diminished. Rooms of the self are walled off. Truth collapses to fit a fictional organising principle we’ve adopted.“

Being an artist means different things. Some aspects can be subjective, but what we know for sure is that you need to learn your craft and broaden your view of the world and other ways of thinking.

One way of doing this too, is reading.

Stay Weird,

<3

title: Art Discipline .21
subtitle: Discipline ò_ó
excerpt: Why Discipline?
body:
Why Discipline?

This newsletter was started with the goal of sharing thoughts on art making, sharing insights from projects I’m developing and games I’m part of.

In general to talk about discipline in art.

Discipline is only necessary when you’re doing something you don’t want to do. You don’t need discipline for things that are purely fun. Most of us start making art because it’s a blast, it’s an outlet for expression and fun ideas. It feels good.

But frustration hits when you see you lack the tools to express certain ideas and these don’t get out of your head properly.

That means it’s time to learn technique, so you start studying things that are harder, need consistency and may be boring sometimes.

That’s the part that requires discipline, every day you carry on with your practice without the promise that you will make it.

But without that discipline and practise, no one makes it as an artist.

Advice and people who suck

There’s something I love about art and it’s that your money or contacts don’t matter, if someone sucks and doesn’t want to put in the work, they will continue to suck.

But remember, art and work (even as an artist) are not the same. So some of these people unfortunately get to important positions working their way up without proper work or with the taste of a monkey’s ass.

I would hesitate on people who give a clear and confident answer on what you should do to improve or to move ahead in your career.

People can give advice (I do too in mentorships, chatting or here lol) but there’s no “path”, there’s just your own experience of the world and what you do with your art.

You find your own path by making art and learning.

Don’t seek clear answers from anyone for an art career, the answer usually is in your practice, work and interests.

What’s going on here ò_ó

As an update on what I’m up to now:

The following drops will be about Megalith, I’m trying to focus as much as possible on the comic book while working on Clash of Clans.

And that’s already a lot, there’s so much I haven’t shared yet from Supercell.

I was trying to do other stuff like Colorpoop, but that was crazy haha. The overload I have been carrying has been too much to move forward.

So I have laser focus on Megalith when it’s about creating, and will be sharing here updates and learnings along this project.

Live and learn, remember that whoever focuses, wins.

<3

body:
In this new drop, I’ve got some news that might interest you, or someone you know, on their artistic journey.

✨ I’ve joined forces with THU (Trojan Horse Was a Unicorn) as part of their mentorship system. ✨

I’m opening a limited offer for 7 artists who want focused, personalized guidance.

How the mentorship works

  • Sessions: 6 individual 1-hour sessions.

  • Frequency and Duration: Up to you — ideally monthly to do a follow up for 6 months.

We’ll analyze your work and define clear next steps based on your profile, goals, and context.

👉 Check the mentorship here

To view the offer, you’ll need a THU account (it’s free).

Any questions or consideration send me a message here or through Instagram.

Mentorship Approach

I believe improvement comes from practice and repetition.

This mentorship is for you if you want to:

  1. Improve your character design skills.

  2. Polish your portfolio so it’s clear and focused.

  3. Learn how to tell a story through your portfolio. How you think is what art directors care about most.

  4. Understand how to think about character design (the key factor that most people miss when building a portfolio).

This is not a rigid program with fixed assignments. Instead, we’ll adapt everything to your goals, your rhythm, and your way of creating.

Each session builds on the previous one: we’ll review progress, identify strengths and weaknesses, and adjust the plan so you always know what to focus on next.

Why Characters?

I love designing almost everything, and I know many of you do too, but characters tend to sit at the center of it all.

They are the foundation of interesting stories. We instinctively turn everything into characters: landscapes, props, even abstract ideas. Our brains are wired to see life everywhere and imagine things coming alive.

Even though I have work on Character design for some time now, this last year I have been specially focused on them, so that’s where I can help the most. Whether your goal is animation or video games (the approach differs, and I’ll adapt to your focus).

A Note on Teaching

I won’t dwell on impostor syndrome (it’s too much of a cliché in art circles) but it hits hard when you consider teaching or showing your process to others.

For a long time, I associated teaching with being above others, and that made me uncomfortable.

Over time, my perspective changed.

Teaching isn’t about hierarchy, it’s about passing knowledge forward and you taking whatever works best for you.

It is just sharing.

This newsletter started as a way to share what I know and what I’m living as an artist.

Through writing, I discovered that I enjoy sharing ideas, developing them, and dissecting how art works for me.

That’s the same mindset I’m bringing into this mentorship.

See you around, stay weird.

title: Art Discipline .18
subtitle: Falling Forward: Risk Feeds Creativity
excerpt: What’s your dream as an artist and what’s the fear that’s keeping you from chasing it?
body:
What’s your dream as an artist and what’s the fear that’s keeping you from chasing it?

The creative path is messy.

We try to predict the right next step, but we can’t. The only thing we can do is act now.

Risks

In a previous Art Discipline issue, I talked about taking risks. Like leaving my first job to go back to Lanzarote, or leaving Roll7 (the studio behind OlliOlli World).

The third one came in 2023, when I decided to leave my last full-time position.

Recently, I found an old note I wrote to myself about this:

“It’s been a bit over a month since I left my position at Yuga Labs as art director to focus on personal projects.

The last 6–7 years I’d been working non-stop. Just moving forward.

Now I’ve been reflecting on my goals as an artist. I get this feeling that I’ve done nothing, and what’s in the past feels like it was made by someone else.

For a moment, stopping the wheel felt like jumping into the void of failure.”

The Real Risk Is Not Moving

Financially, leaving was terrifying.

Creatively, the real risk was staying.

It was my first Art Director role, with a salary I never imagined earning but I wasn’t happy. I was barely making art, and what little I did didn’t feel mine.

So I weighed it:

  • Short term: money, stability. Also ego, thinking being AD really mattered something. I was betraying my believing that titles are crap, just what you do matters.

  • Long term: wasting my best years on projects I didn’t believe in.

I had savings, and art came first. I’d rather earn less and feel proud of my work than look back at a portfolio that felt like someone else’s.

So I jumped into the void.

A year later

Here’s what that “terrifying future” actually looked like:

  • Read a shit ton of books.

  • Finished the first chapter of Megalith.

  • Launched Art Discipline.

  • Worked on Colorpoop (update on this soon x_x).

  • Joined UMA Games for some time and travelled with them to Tuscany.

  • Illustrated a story for Tales Up (mobile game by Periple Studio).

  • Created character designs for a Korean TV show (that flopped).

  • Pitched Megalith at Weird Market (Animation fest in Valencia, Spain).

  • Started learning Blender.

At the time, none of this felt like “success.” Just small daily steps: reading, drawing, learning, saying yes to curiosity.

Looking back now, that scary pause became the space I needed to grow to make work that felt like mine, to explore, and eventually to join Clash of Clans at Supercell.

So, why this matters?

Every creative reaches a point where comfort starts to dull their edge. We know what we want to do, but the step toward it usually demands a sacrifice and discipline to keep advancing, even when it’s uncomfortable.

If you stopped today and looked back at your last two years of art, would you feel proud?

If not, what’s one small step you could take this week to realign with the work that feels truly yours?

Will you feel proud two years from now?

Stay Creative, Stay Weird.

title: Art Discipline .17
subtitle: Look for Your Own Way: Creating Art for Everdale
excerpt: Nothing Beats Bathroom Breaks
body:
Nothing Beats Bathroom Breaks

This drop is about how doing things your way can actually be what gets you the job. Using the mobile game, Everdale, as an example of how weird art, personal taste, and favorite subjects (like buildings) ended up being exactly what Supercell needed.

During one of my first jobs in a Nickelodeon show, I had two great moments throughout the day:

  • A bowl of cereal.

  • Bathroom breaks that took a bit longer playing Supercell games.

What would you love to create but you’re avoiding?

At the time, I was working as a layout artist in animation, kind of boring. My dream was to be a concept artist in games.

One thing I really liked was environment concept art. I was doing backgrounds for animation already but I liked some weird vibes I wasn’t fully embracing, wasn’t listening to my inner voice.

Until the day I did, and created some weird buildings and props like these:

Just draw what you love

A year later, after a lot of work building my portfolio and putting artworks out there I got contacted for Valorant (talked about it in the previous newsletter) and then as that started I got another project as a concept artist.

In 2019 I got the opportunity to do concept art for Everdale, at that time Supercell’s next game. Working with Zombot Studio.

Turns out those weird concepts I was doing on my own got me somewhere.

I shared with you what turned my career around: stopped doing what I thought a concept artist’s portfolio should look like and started creating what felt right to me:

There are different weirder approaches I was taking towards environment and character design. In this project the environment part was very important, they needed to explore and try out stuff.

I focused on building designs, something during that time was one of my favourite things to draw.

Art for Everdale

Here’s a case of one of the concepts I was developing )full project in my Artstation)

Here I explore the shape language, colors and materials for these Capitol buildings.

We were in an early exploration phase so you will see there’s some iteration on the shapes. Like this image, starting to create a modular system:

The main shapes I was using in the beginning were looking too primitive so we checked some real buildings to mix a bit the shapes, breaking the big cubes. Also added some architectural details to show a different vibe for this since it was a campus/library.

Exploring again different building shapes and structure (with some notes I received):

Kept exploring these adding the base to integrate more with the environment and expand on some details:

Here are some notes from Supercell to keep pushing and mixing some of the concepts:

Last iteration before I had to jump to other concepts:

As you can see most of the time is an iteration on details and splitting hairs to nail the design. But getting the right shapes and colors is what makes the bigger difference when iterating.

title: Art Discipline .16
subtitle: Tattooing Oranges and Riot Games
excerpt: Tattoo and Oranges
body:
Tattoo and Oranges

One summer, broke and frustrated, I bought a tattoo machine and started tattooing oranges.

I was doing crappy freelance jobs here and there, earning maybe €300 a month. Some clients tried to trick me; one didn’t pay (a now well-known game outsourcing studio).

Also bought my first squatty potty, but let’s continue.

I kept sending my portfolio around every day and making new artworks.

Meanwhile my savings were disappearing, and my hopes of breaking through as a concept artist were fading.

Then an email arrived: West Studio.

First Shot

West was reaching out about a big project.

I joined the call and one of the art directors I admired (Mingchen Shen) was there.

My English wasn’t great, and I didn’t think my portfolio was there yet, so yeah, I was nervous.

But I did my best to play it cool.
Don’t look desperate please.

Big project, kind people, and good money.

I didn’t fully believe it until the contract arrived a couple of days later.

Then my career changed, I started working on creating art for Valorant (Riot Games) with West Studio.

Avoiding Concept Art, Again.

Valorant was my first proper job in games (thank you, West Studio). It’s funny because if you look at my work, it doesn’t match the game style at first.

You never know all the different needs of the art for a game and the opportunities these can bring, even the apparently small ones.

West contacted me to work specifically on Sprays. But that kind of task opened the door to bigger asignments for the game like Props, Environment Art and full Illustrations.

I mentioned the importance of building a unique portfolio, not just doing concept art, but growing as an artist outside that box.

A personal project I made for fun (Meaningless Adventure) got me visibility online and then my first work opportunites landed.

It wasn’t really one project or one post; it was the compound effect of years of making things and showing them.

Here’s what came from that attention. This was the first one.

Art for Valorant

Initially I was hired to produce Sprays, (“Graffitis” you can use during a match in Valorant to paint on surfaces):

After delivering those, I got to work on new stuff like Gun Buddies:

These are charms to decorate your weapon:

Then came prop design and rendering:

This was tricky because I had to render realistically, something I was trying to avoid on my own work.

But luckily it was a skill I had in my toolkit. Very handy to know in production.
(I will share with you what I believe every artist should learn)

Later, a huge challenge with environment concept art:

I was sweating blood painting this.

Then came some player card illustrations. Really fun to make and I learnt a lot:

Closing the Loop

This was the chance I’d been waiting for. Once it arrived I did everything I could to deliver.

More opportunities came around the same time, will share those experiences too.

Even though sometimes waiting for the one shot can be frustrating, be patient and keep going.

Work now so that when the opportunity arrives, you’re ready.

title: Art Discipline .15
subtitle: Finding Your Voice as an Artist
excerpt: Art Discipline is a monthly publication to learn about art in the game industry. Dive into character design, world building, and creativity.
body:
Art Discipline is a monthly publication to learn about art in the game industry. Dive into character design, world building, and creativity.

Ever feel like that? When creating something doesn’t click?

I’ve been stuck there for a while with illustration.

And I’ve started to figure out why.

This drop might help if you’re not finding your voice.

Concept Art: A Strength That Becomes a Limitation

For the last few years, I’ve worked primarily in video games, specifically doing concept art and visual development.

This is about creating the preproduction of the game, building the world; and then solving problems as they appear during production.

The artwork you create is not an end by itself, it’s a piece inside a bigger picture. It’s a tool. A stepping stone for something else.

That means that a concept doesn’t need to look polished and ready to consume.

Concept art teaches you to think inside a product.

Working as a concept artist makes you a better designer and allows you to develop your own visual style by repetition. Creating characters, props and environments over and over gets to grow your visual library.

Repetition built confidence.

But it also built habit.

But here is the issue: concept art is never the final product.

In concept art, your job is to serve something bigger.

In illustration, your image is the story. It has to speak for itself.

And when I make an illustration, I get stuck on the same process.

Illustration is a Different Beast

An illustration is a storytelling piece by itself that an audience will experience.

Finding your voice in this aspect is what I feel it’s missing in my own work.

The same process I use for concept art doesn’t work when I try to illustrate a print, comic panels, or even t-shirts.

Working on a final product directly for an audience is different than creating concept art for an entertainment project.

Context is Everything

In entertainment we tend to frame illustrations like a movie shot.

Cinematic shots feel safe but they’re not always right for every format like an illustration to print or comic panels.

The freedom to tell a visual story is wider.

I always found difficult to find my own voice for illustration, to tell stories with images with a visual way that looked solid to me.

Meaning, the final look: line art, colors, visual treatment.

Honestly, that’s part of why I don’t sell prints.

Because I don’t think my art pieces are strong enough to live on their own, for now.

This is because of 2 reasons,

  1. The content of the pieces. What are you trying to say?

  2. The form, the how. Every context and format requires a unique treatment. A style frame for animation needs a different approach than a print to hang on a gallery, or a t-shirt to wear.

Every art form speaks their own language.

For example in illustration for printing, this is a no for me:

And this works better:

With prints, I’m thinking aesthetics first.

Tighter compositions. More graphic. Bolder ideas.

What to Explore

Identify the areas where you are not happy with your art, maybe is the way you storyboard, or create character designs. Think on treatments and techniques to try.

There are 2 contexts where I need to work on my art:

  • Prints, using the aesthetic principle we just mentioned (very taste based).

  • Comic panels to tell short funny stories: this was my initial goal with Colorpoop. But I have been afraid of doing it.

There’s a huge range of possibilities to explore and find your own way.

As artists we all wrestle with this too at different stages.

I will share experiments and how to try to explore this aspects and find a solution.

See you in the next drop <3

title: Art Discipline .14
subtitle: How to Make an Impactful Artwork for Supercell
excerpt: Art Discipline is a monthly publication to learn about art in the game industry from the artist behind OlliOlli World, currently at Supercell. Dive into character design, world building, and creativity. Stay creative, Stay weird.
body:
Art Discipline is a monthly publication to learn about art in the game industry from the artist behind OlliOlli World, currently at Supercell. Dive into character design, world building, and creativity. Stay creative, Stay weird.

A lot of creatives panic when facing a big brief.

Earlier this year, Supercell reached out to create an illustration to celebrate their 15th anniversary.

To capture 5 games, 15 years and countless screaming Barbarians.

All in a single image.

Here’s how I broke it down and what you can apply to your own work when facing a big task.

Funny detail: I was already working on Clash of Clans but this was a separate team within the company.

Creative Paralysis

This kind of project causes creative paralysis because you may try to solve everything at once.

How to solve this Paralysis by Analysis in this case?

Break the problem down.

From abstract → visual

From big → small

Focus on the thing that has the most impact to the viewer and will be the fundamental for the artwork: Composition.

Ask yourself these questions:

  1. What do you want to tell?

  2. What feeling do you want to express?

  3. How should the viewer experience the image?

Sometimes working for a key art for a game you may want to express the possibilities of the game itself.

For example:

  • Enhancing the exploration part of it if it’s an open world game.

  • Maybe you want to express the mysteries that a specific world got for you to try to unfold.

  • Sometimes you need to show key gameplay aspects. In OlliOlli World the fact that you skateboard through a path exploring a crazy world had to be seen and understood in a single image.

What was my goal here?

To show the craziness of Supercell’s worlds in a playful, funny way. Following their sense of humour.

Let the viewer travel through the illustration, discovering little stories like you would do in their games, and enjoy the cool characters Supercell has created over the years.

I started sketching whatever popped into my head, chasing the first instinct.

(You can go check inspiration to get rolling first if feeling stuck.)

Finding the Right Format

Some early ideas looked nice but didn’t work.

I considered a cinematic shot but it felt off. Supercell already has cinematic material.

But the answer was in front of me: go isometric.

  1. It mirrors their games POV.

  2. It lets me build multiple tiny scenes.

  3. No visual hierarchy with the different IPs.

This gave me a visual framework to start building the world.

Process (Without losing your mind)

Once I had the layout, I built a reference board:

Time to sketch and send it over.

Approved by the client.

Now the fun part, hundreds of hours of line art:

Coloring Nightmare

Color came next. The file was huge (1.5 meters height for print)

So I broke it down:

  1. Flat colors to block zones and set the mood.

  2. Cool-toned palette with warm accents.

  3. Focus on clarity, color has to help the composition and feeling you want to share with the viewer.

Shadow pass: Multiply layer + mask. Quick, editable, and no mess when revisiting.

Then came the fun stuff:

  • Glows.

  • Highlights.

  • Depth tricks.

  • Make the image feel alive.

Story First

Skill makes something look good.

But creating the story is what makes it matter.

You can render a beautiful image.

But if it doesn’t say anything, it vanishes.

A good story gets remembered.

Stay Creative,

title: Art Discipline .13
subtitle: AI: Shit Floats
excerpt: Art Discipline is a monthly drop of thoughts, processes, and behind-the-scenes from the artist behind OlliOlli World (BAFTA-nominated). Dive into character design, world building, and the weird joys of making art. Stay weird.
body:
Art Discipline is a monthly drop of thoughts, processes, and behind-the-scenes from the artist behind OlliOlli World (BAFTA-nominated). Dive into character design, world building, and the weird joys of making art. Stay weird.

Hating AI as a general term and a technology that could enhance some aspects of our lives is questionable and up to debate. But when it comes to AI generating images and doing the “creative process” for you, well, I got some thoughts.

When we talk about the creative process and why AI image generators are fundamentally not just a “new tool” I separate this topic into different parts:

  1. Creativity Can’t Be Outsourced: Skipping the steps of a creative process and not controlling the outcome. Atrophy of skills.

  2. Art & Accessibility

  3. Tools: Is ordering from a restaurant like cooking something yourself?

  4. Ethical issues with Copyright Infringement (I won’t expand on this since AI companies steal our data and copyright, there’s not much to add here)

Creativity Can’t Be Outsourced

Creativity and working on art projects is about the journey. You challenge your brain and your knowledge by working on something. Doing that process you materialize how far can you get with your skills. In other words, you can see the gap between your actual skills and the perception in your mind of what you can achieve. This process makes your brain work, think creatively on what you can do and get ideas during the process.

Why not pressing a button and getting a final thing, like an image or a video?

If you describe with words what you want, it should give you something accurate, right?

This sounds like ordering from a restaurant, you’re not making it.

Reality is more complicated than that, the creative process is not just “you have an image in your brain and you want to express it” or “take a couple of things you like and mix them randomly”.

When you take a couple of things as references and you want to mix them to create something new, one could say that it makes sense to put them in a mixer, press a button and ready to go.

On one hand, anyone can do that so where’s the merit on that?

This is one of the arguments pro AI creating images: AI does the same as the human brain, mixes images or ideas from others and creates something new.

But there’s a key question most people forget. When an artist take references and create a project base on these, the process goes through the artist’s mind, filtering the world and projecting their personality into the project. This is what creates style, happy accidents and gives room to experimentation. Something that just can be achieved by experiencing the process of creating something.

But it’s not your brain doing the work. You’re typing some words and pressing a button hoping for the best. You’re not learning, you don’t know how to modify an image to achieve what you want. Skills atrophy if you don’t use them.

You can’t outsource creativity, once it’s not going through your brain, is not going to be you.

Art & Accessibility

There’re talks about art being accessible with AI, about “democratization of creativity”. What does this even mean? What’s creativity? What does it mean to be democratized?

Art is already accessible, take a pen and write your story or draw a doodle. You suck? Learn from others. Information is what’s been democratized thanks to the internet and we can use it in our advantage. But there’s always a price and in the case of creating something the price is hard work.

Everything can’t be free.

To achieve some things you need to learn your craft and develop skills. This is not a waste of time. These are paths to mastery and getting a deeper understanding of the art you want to express your ideas in.

Learning your craft and the process involved in creating a piece of art gives you power to create what’s in your mind.

Independence means freedom to create.

Tools: Is ordering from a restaurant like cooking something yourself?

We all have heard repeatedly about this comparison of AI with other tools in the past that produced a revolution.

“Is just another tool, adapt or die.”

There’s a universal law with humans, and it’s that we don’t want to see reality if we suck big time at something.

Most people think that they have great vision and taste.

This is a big majority of people so it makes sense that generative AI had such a big welcome. All of this people with great taste and no knowledge can type down a prompt and ask for something thinking it’s because of them that this image exists.

The trick of the century.

This is also easy to do and gives you a hit of dopamine so it’s the perfect combination.

Can this be a tool?

Maybe, if we remove the copyright infringement and scraping the data from all the internet I can see some uses. In the creative process I think it affects in a very negative way because of the reasons explained earlier.

Maybe in the future as part of a brainstorming session combining your own work?

Maybe just as part of some early explorations but never as the final thing?

Maybe to use it for technical aspects like correcting the light in your image the same way you would ask for feedback to another person?

A lot of open questions in that regard, but about the creative process I got no doubts. Laziness tends to win and we will miss some amazing art because of this.

Creativity is about the actual journey, not the destination.

See you in the next drop <3

body:
Art Discipline is a monthly drop of thoughts, processes, and behind-the-scenes from the artist behind OlliOlli World (BAFTA-nominated). Dive into character design, world building, and the weird joys of making art. Stay weird.

Avoiding Concept Art

As an artist, you’ve probably had moments where you don’t know what the hell you’re doing. You’re stuck, questioning every move, feeling like if your next piece doesn’t hit, you’re doomed.

Most of us end up doing what we think is expected. We make stuff that fits a certain studio, a certain job title, or a certain box.

But I will tell you otherwise:

Want to be a concept artist? Avoid concept art. Avoid games.

This affects how we approach our creative journey and how we spend our time creating. We tend to overthink this process of starting a new thing based on many ideas and external factors. But these are critical moments when you have many possibilities. It doesn’t matter if it “fails.” Action builds momentum. It trains your creative instinct.

Let me tell you about a small project, one of those that without any expectations changed a whole career.

I’ve talked about taking risks before. This time, I want to show you what that actually looked like and how one weird little detour got me into the entertainment industry.

Any action compounds over time, and this one made a huge difference.

Portfolio Graveyard

Like many of you, I spent a lot of time building a portfolio around what I thought concept art was supposed to look like. I was learning to paint, draw traditionally, and mess around with basic 3D blockouts, trying to hit all the right marks.

I actually enjoyed making these pieces. But the more I looked around, the more I realized what really pulled me in was the animation industry. Specifically the stylization, the simplification, the clarity. Art could be cool and simple, straight to the point of telling a story or sharing an idea in a simple (not easy) way.

After months of sending my portfolio out there and hearing crickets, I decided to make a small project for my portfolio based on what I liked. Not what I thought studios needed. No one was hiring me so f*ck it, at least I could have some fun while sinking in my art career.

That’s when I decided to make a project just for myself. No rules. No expectations. Not what I thought studios wanted, just what I wanted to see. A series of illustrations telling a story visually.

I didn’t overthink this, I designed the characters and went for the frames where I designed the environments also as an excuse to design some strange places with architecture I liked and exploring different color palettes.

In the next drop I will share, the project I’ve been refering to, titled: Meaningless Adventure.

(There’re some size limitations of email, and I want to share the whole thing ._.)

What about Concept Art?

Now you might be thinking: “What does any of this have to do with concept art?”

The important aspect of this project is that shows my way of thinking about funny and silly art while showing my thought process designing from scratch and using visual storytelling.

Thanks mostly to this project I started gaining visibility and work inquiries. Doesn’t mean it was a lottery ticket. I had been working and sharing my stuff for years. But this was the one that clicked with people. One of those “years to become an overnight success” situations.

I thought it was a silly project just for fun and that it wouldn’t serve as something in my portfolio. Turned to be all the way around.

Do what you love and try to improve with it.

I threw it online without expectations, and it caught fire (in my small scale). Visibility grew. A few months later, I started getting real opportunities:

Valorant (Riot Games), Everdale (Supercell), Hourglass Moonland (Animated show), etc.

I’ll go deeper into those projects in future drops. Some were wins, some were flops, but most were visually and creatively connected to Meaningless Adventure.

Should you actually avoid the whole concept art vibe?

Not really. But I do think you should look beyond the game industry for inspiration.

Because this personal project is part of what led me to make the art for OlliOlli World. A whole game in my own art style.

Part of luck and good timing and part of me making the decision to do something I purely liked and I put out there not caring if it helped my “concept artist portfolio”.

I don’t give a crap about what technically makes a good concept art portfolio.
You have to show your taste, your skills, and your ideas.
That’s what makes a good concept artist.

We’ll talk more about skills and technical stuff in future drops.

But for now, tell stories. Don’t just design things for the sake of designing.
We all want to see what you’ve got to tell.

Thanks for reading and see you in the next drop to see Meaningless Adventure.

excerpt: Art Discipline is a monthly drop of thoughts, processes, and behind-the-scenes from the artist behind OlliOlli World (BAFTA-nominated). Dive into character design, world building, and the weird joys of making art. Stay weird.
body:
Art Discipline is a monthly drop of thoughts, processes, and behind-the-scenes from the artist behind OlliOlli World (BAFTA-nominated). Dive into character design, world building, and the weird joys of making art. Stay weird.

You are not going to get taught how to get ideas and design cool stuff. There’s always magic surrounding it.

But let’s try to pull back the curtain anyway.

Breaking Down the Creative Process_

When it comes to designing/drawing/creating, you can break it into two parts:

  • Technical sh*t: the how we make the stuff that’s in our head a reality. Easier to explain and easier to break down into steps.

  • Creative sh*t: the why, the what, the fun. More difficult to materialize and to explain in a clear way.

The latter is more abstract, but we will do our best to break it down here.

There are tons of tutorials and courses that teach technique, sculpting, drawing, modeling, animating, etc.

Those are the mediums to pour your creativity (technique is developing the skills to use those mediums).

This drop is about that other side: The ideas, expressing them regardless of your medium of choice.

Find those ideas (I mean it, run, find them)_

Sure, you can take notes, snap reference photos, or write down thoughts. But if you're working in a visual medium, you'll need to sketch. It's the clearest way to develop, test, and express ideas.

Sketching matters on a few levels:

  1. Thumbnails for an illustration. Storyboards for a film. Quick visuals that lay the groundwork.

  2. When learning to represent the real world and translate it into a 2D plane like paper we need sketching. Fast, low-pressure iterations build feedback loops. You learn faster when you sketch a lot.

Sketching can be used for studies, learning how something works and understanding their shapes (like a tree, a car, or the human body). Or it can be used for dumping ideas on paper to brainstorm and train our idea making part of the brain.

This last part I think is the most important as an artist and the one I spend the most time working on at the moment (after spending years working on the fundamentals — will talk about this in the future).

It’s better to start with a good idea and crappy execution than the other way around. If the idea is fun, you’re already halfway there.

Sketching Practice Framework_

Separate your sketching sessions that are for pure practice into 2 categories:

  • Idea dumping: Have fun, force your mind to try new things. Explore those weird ideas*.

  • Analytical Studies: Try to understand how something works. Don’t just copy what you see. Break it down. Understand it so you can build a visual library in your brain and draw from imagination. There’s a huge difference here between intention and drawing brainless just copying what you see. Save your energy and focus.

*and share them so we can see how weird you are.

Burning ideas_

Get those ideas out of your brain, sketch and dump. Build that cool collection of silliness.

Here are some from my digital sketchbook - I will do a proper post with my traditional sketchbooks.

These kids didn’t enjoy my sketches but I hope you’re more merciful.

Part of my digital Sketchpoop:

These are some of the digital sketches I do for fun (iPad sheets where I push ideas for practice using the kind of humour I want in my artworks). I should experiment more with the way I do things but most of these are about drawing ideas and getting them out of my brain.

Thank you and until the next drop :)

excerpt: Art Discipline is a monthly drop of thoughts, process, and behind-the-scenes from the artist behind OlliOlli World (BAFTA-nominated). Dive into character design, world building, and the weird joys of making art. Stay weird.
body:
Art Discipline is a monthly drop of thoughts, process, and behind-the-scenes from the artist behind OlliOlli World (BAFTA-nominated). Dive into character design, world building, and the weird joys of making art. Stay weird.

There’s an attraction toward characters. That’s why we spend hours in games playing with the customization menus or buying accesories just to make them look cooler, more us.

Environments can tell stories and set a mood, but we don’t connect to them in the same way we do with characters. The effort is not symmetrical on how easily we read them.

Sure, people get excited exploring a beautiful environment but there’s a different hierarchy when it comes to empathy.

“Wow, what a game! So many options!”

Characters Create the Context

Now: What does the following scene make you feel?

And now?

Okay, maybe I tricked you with not the best example. You can add a dead body to anything and it changes the vibe.

How about this:

Now you have more info like how deep is the river, oh well…

Nevermind, I tried.

My point is: you can keep the same lighting, the same birds, the same trees. But as soon as a character enters the frame, everything changes. Your brain starts creating a story, trying to fill in the gaps, to understand.

Sometimes we can play with this by choosing how much we show, or by revealing something that makes the viewer reframe what they thought they knew. That’s the invisible duel between storyteller and spectator.

It’s like when a friend tells you something that happened to them but most people are brief or don’t give all the details so your brain starts filling in the blanks automatically. Like, how people were dressed, the color of the cars, anything really.

Last drop, I shared an overview of Megalith, the comic I’m making with Lizz Lunney. In the journey of our heroes, we introduce a wide cast of characters. Some directly impact the main storyline; others just shift your perception of the world.

Every character adds a piece to the larger puzzle of the universe.

Setting Your Mind to Design Characters

This drop shows some broader ideas about character design, in future drops we will get deeper into more specific aspects of character design. This is the topic I get more requests for in socials or in my mentorship sessions/portfolio reviews. We will also see practical cases of designs I have made for video game and animation projects that you may have played or watched :)

The process starts with the idea: who is this character, what’s their context, and what are they about?

I explore different shapes to see what feels right. A mix of exploration and intuition.

Once we are happy with the visual design (this process goes through different iterations that I will cover in another drop), the character gets reinforced by the acting (poses, expressions, how they deliver lines). I try not to overthink, trusting what feels right is key.

Sometimes the process goes in reverse, I explore characters thinking about the world we are creating and some catches Lizz’s attention so she takes that design to inspire a character in development for the story. We have had many cases like this where We feed off each other’s creative process.

Like one of our characters from Megalith, Donnie Voyaggio:

I created this character sheet exploring some characters on what I felt could be right for this story. Then Lizz thought this guy was right for a character she had in mind and we moved forward with it.

I rewatched Twin Peaks recently, and it’s amazing how each character is built. They’re strange, mysterious, and memorable. David Lynch is a master at building characters that stand out (even before they speak).

Of course, characters don’t exist in a vacuum. The environment and other elements (like sound) also set the mood.

Characters are mostly built through actions and dialogue but we get the added layer of design. We can tell a story visually before the character even moves.

That’s always my goal in character design: to create visual storytelling that sparks curiosity, even in stillness. A design that speaks before the character says a word.

Don’t limit your character creation to what’s traditionally “the correct way”. Do what your taste dictates and stay weird.

This newsletter is for you so if there’s something you’re struggling with in your character design work, reply and let me know. I might cover it in a future drop.

body:
Hey there, Germán here 🌞!

We missed each other last month and I really missed this moment of sharing some stuff with you. February was intense, I spent the whole month in Helsinki working at the Supercell offices (I started working in Clash of Clans last November! Hopefully I will share some cool stuff I’ve been working on with you here) and then got super sick x_x

Incredible experience, here we are now and I wanted to take this time to talk a bit and reflect about one of the projects I am working on, our comic book, Megalith.

Recently I was rewatching Akira Kurosawa’s speech from the 1990 Oscars, where he received an honorary award. At one point, he says:

“… I don’t feel that I understand cinema yet … but what I promise you is that from now on I will work as hard as I can at making movies and maybe by following this path I will achieve an understanding of the true essence of cinema and earn this award.”

Wtf, right? We live in a world where so many people act as if they know everything (and thanks to that attitude, they often get their way) and then you have Kurosawa, an actual legend, saying this with humility.

For a moment, I wondered if writing this newsletter was like claiming I do understand art. But then realized this is a way of trying to understand it one day, hopefully.

The only way to get closer to understanding art is to do the actual work. The work is how you show the world what you think about art and life.

A few drops back, I talked about public speaking and a presentation I gave at an entertainment event.

Today I want to talk about the project I was presenting.

Megalith, the comic book I’m co-developing with the writer Lizz Lunney. We worked together building the world of the video game OlliOlli World. After finishing working on the game we decided to join forces to create our own IP and tell a story that truly matters to us.

Megalith Islands: A Journey into a New Universe

This is a story that follows the adventure of two friends in a fantasy world.

Dji and Skit sail across the seven Megalith Islands in a tale of friendship, creativity, and overcoming challenges, told through this unusual and humorous world.

Little is known about the origins of the seven Megalith Islands, but these two reckless friends are about to uncover secrets hidden in the depths of the world as they embark on a journey that will change them forever.

These two best friends embark on a mission triggered by a family event. In the first chapter, Skit’s aunt passes away, and they have to travel in search of the inheritance, which is a family legacy.

From here, they decide to leave the capital island and travel through the archipelago.

On their journey, they encounter a constellation of unique characters and are swept into an adventure that, ultimately, strengthens their friendship and changes the way they view their own roles in the world.

An interesting detail we explore in the story is how the distant past can still affect us in ways we can’t expect (weird concept but can be interesting and fun).

Skit suffers from hallucinations and dissociation from reality. This is something the character discovers throughout the story. It’s a hereditary condition and appears as a reaction to their fear of the sea, probably inherited from an ancestor who had a maritime accident.

This will be developed throughout the comic.

Returning to a more global vision of the project:

This fantastic world is rooted in ancient Ireland and the Canary Islands. We’re taking some ideas from the culture and folklore of these places, where both of us are from, to inspire us in creating parts of this world.

There will be a lot of nautical themes starting in chapter two, so expect many designs of strange ships.

We’ve completed the first chapter, and we’re currently starting the second. The project will consist of 8 chapters with an approximate total of 160 pages.

The project is progressing while we both continue to work in the video game industry.

Creating the IP in comic form is the most accessible way to validate the story. But one of the next steps, as I mentioned earlier, will be to prepare a pitch deck and animation proposal for the project.

This is something we both have experience with.

I don’t believe much in simplifications when it’s about stories since there’s a lot of details, characters, moments, etc. which enrich this experience. But for now this is the best way to get the gist of this project.

One of the conclusions we reached after working together on OlliOlli World was that we could build a fun world with an interesting narrative. With Megalith, we want to apply those skills to our own world, with a slightly more serious backdrop, while maintaining that laid-back touch.

In the meantime, we’re sharing the process on our Patreon as we keep working on this project and developing the story. Chapter one is completely in there if you want to give it a read.

You can read the first chapter and access patron posts by subscribing for one month and then unsubscribing. No need to keep a longer subscription if you just want to check out the first chapter:

https://www.patreon.com/MegalithIslands

Now we are working on the second chapter after sending the first to a loooot of publishers and agents to get some feedback on it. We are making this story happen no matter what :)

title: Art Discipline .07
subtitle: Digital Playground and Slow Productivity
excerpt: Welcome to a new drop of Art Discipline, my name is Germán and here I share insights, processes, and updates from my creative journey. This edition is packed with reflections on slow productivity, a breakdown of my current projects, and a sneak peek at the design process for my future website.
body:
Welcome to a new drop of Art Discipline, my name is Germán and here I share insights, processes, and updates from my creative journey. This edition is packed with reflections on slow productivity, a breakdown of my current projects, and a sneak peek at the design process for my future website.

If you want just to see the website project initial mockups go to the bottom section! There’s a whole design process behind it and I will unfold the first steps for this project.

My Current Projects

The new year is all about focus, cutting out the noise and doubling down on what matters.

Last year, I started working at Supercell, I’m extremely excited about the opportunity to work with so many amazing people. It’s also a challenge I was looking forward to, as an artist to design and propose ideas for Clash of Clans.

So I’m working in a bunch of my own projects at the same time while working at Supercell and learning Blender to become a 3D beast (kidding, but no kidding). This means the window of time for my own projects is very narrow and I have to be efficient to move forward and not burning out.

The projects I got in hands are these:

  • Megalith (Comic Book): Co-developing this long-term project with writer Lizz Lunney. Twice a year, I dedicate focused sprints to creating pages and artwork.

  • Colorpoop (Short Film): A personal story brought to life in collaboration with animator Opensandwich. With storyboards and animatics almost done, I’m currently prepping animation sheets as we progress through rough animation. This will likely take 2–3 years to complete.

  • Art Discipline (Newsletter): I didn’t think about this as a project. But it takes time, surprise! I try to make this as a window to see cool shit in the process or sharing thoughts. But sometimes I get carried away and each drop can take time. Monthly basis.

  • Website with store: The most immediate project on my plate. This will serve as a hub for my art and include a store to sell art products. It’s a short-term project (6–10 months) but an essential step for supporting my broader goals.

My way of working to achieve these is prioritizing what really is important at the moment and strictly helps the whole thing advance. Some examples:

  • I write newsletter drafts whenever inspiration strikes, ensuring I always have something in the pipeline (I try to match it to what I’m working on that month).

  • With Colorpoop, I work in cycles, creating animation sheets every couple of months based on Opensandwich’s completed shots.

When it’s about my projects I don’t care about speed, it’s about slow productivity and making meaningful progress.

Slow Productivity: Book Book Book!

I had a season of following Cal Newport’s work, reading some of his books. Between those, I read Slow Productivity. Probably the most meaningful to help me reflect and think on the stuff I do and what is really meaningful to me as an artist.

At its core, the book argues that meaningful progress comes not from doing everything, but from doing the right things, slowly and with intention. Here are the three main principles:

  1. Do fewer things: Prioritize what’s truly important and cut the rest.

  2. Work at a natural pace: Quality takes time, so avoid rushing.

  3. Obsess over quality: Focus deeply on fewer projects to create something truly exceptional.

These ideas might seem straightforward, but the book’s anecdotes and strategies give more context and background to these concepts.

Some paragraphs to think on the reasons why we voluntarily choose to add more stuff to our to-do list:

“The Industrial Revolution stripped away those last vestiges of variation in our work efforts. The powered mill, followed by the factory, made every day a harvest day - continuous, monotonous labor that never alters. Gone were the seasonal changes and sense-making rituals.”

“It seems like the benefits of technology have created the ability to stack more into our day and onto our schedules than we have the capacity to handle while maintaining a level of quality which makes the things worth doing… I think that’s where the burnout really hurts - when you want to care about something but you’re removed from the capacity to do the thing or do it properly and give it your passion and full attention and creativity because you’re expected to do so many other things.”

Newport also suggests breaking goals into manageable layers:

  • Missions (Big Goals): No more than three overarching goals at a time.

  • Projects: Specific tasks that serve those big goals.

  • Daily Goals: Small, actionable steps to make steady progress.

For example, my “big goals” this year are completing major milestones for Megalith, advancing Colorpoop, and launching my website. Everything I do, like the monthly newsletters ties back to these missions.

“A key tenet of slow productivity is that grand achievement is built on the steady accumulation of modest results over time.”

“The key to meaningful work is in the decision to keep returning to the efforts you find important. Not in getting everything right every time.”

Website Process: First Steps into My Digital Playground

Building a website is like designing a game. It’s interactive, visual, and can be fun or it can be a frustrating piece of shit. I’m trying to avoid the latter lol.

I’ve been messing around with the idea of creating something a bit more interactive like a game. Decided that my website at first has to have a balance between display and functionality. This has to be a reflection of what I like and how I think about a project but also has to be clear and easy to use. In the end the goal is showing my art to you without friction.

My work tends to be a bit silly, so I didn’t want to overdo it with the format and layout of the web to try to achieve a slick look. It is a matter of contrast.

The mockups are in their first phase, and I´m getting the help of Rocío Batanero (designer) to refine the ideas and work on new ones for the site.

The homepage is anchored by a dramatic visual: a character, Ra, floating while stabbed by a giant pencil. Hovering over the menu with the cursor adds playful interactions, like subtle changes to Ra.

I explored different options for the render and decided to go for a more dramatic lighting to match the concept and give the overall look a foggy mood with some noise and extra blurs.

The biggest challenge is figuring out how to present my projects. The first project I’ll feature is OlliOlli World, as it’s my most significant piece of work. The idea is to create a scrolling gallery that combines concept art, designs, and a sense of the project’s scale.

This section is all about immersion, letting you explore the depth and magnitude of the work while keeping navigation smooth.

Another exciting part of the site will be the Concept Store, where I’ll offer art products. Right now, I’m prototyping items like T-shirts, prints, and other goodies. The store will evolve as I develop more concepts and experiment with how to translate my work into tangible pieces.

Over the next few months, I’ll share updates as the site and other projects take shape. I’m excited to create a digital space that’s as fun and engaging as the art I want to share with you. Stay tuned for more behind-the-scenes sneak peeks!

Thanks for being part of this journey, see you soon with more weirdness. Feel free to share thoughts and comments :)

title: Art Discipline .05
subtitle: Taking risks in your career D:
excerpt: I´ve been thinking a lot about the countless paths you can take in creative fields. Each path has its own challenges and opportunities, and there’s often no clear right or wrong choice. When you start learning something new, you quickly realize how much you didn’t know.
body:
I´ve been thinking a lot about the countless paths you can take in creative fields. Each path has its own challenges and opportunities, and there’s often no clear right or wrong choice. When you start learning something new, you quickly realize how much you didn’t know.

Like many of you, I´ve been always drawing. I started studying engineering (why? D:), dropped after 2 years (not an easy moment) and went to study fine arts. No clear idea about the path to become an artist working in games, but I was learning whatever I could online and from people with similar interests I met at uni. After those years I was doing concepts like this:

Throughout my years in the Video Game and Animation industries, some of my best experiences and opportunities have come from taking what are traditionally seen as big stupid risks.

Leaving a stable job and focusing on creating.

In general as an artist I’ve been always looking for time where I can expand my knowledge and producing weird shit drawing or painting freely, that later on I could leverage in my portfolio. Using properly my time it´s been my priority, nothing like the present to create stuff.

Guys, personal projects are projects. They are valid. You don’t need to get paid to do something cool (well, getting paid would be optimal, I know).

One of my first projects that got me a proper portfolio was a project I did with other artists and no funding. Las Niñas Terribles’ shortfilm, more about this in the future.

1. Breaking Into Concept Art

When I first started, I struggled to find a job. After many rejections, I decided to take any art-related job I could find. Luckily, I landed a position as a Layout Artist for a Nickelodeon show. It wasn’t my dream job, but it was a step in the right direction. After a few months, I left due to personal reasons and returned home to the Canary Islands, where there were no studios and no opportunities in the creative field.

2. Creating Meaningful Work

Back home, (thinking that professionally I was dead) I was trying to get freelance work and also I focused on building a portfolio with projects that excited me, I stopped trying to produce the concept art that “I was supposed to have in my portfolio”. Like this:

One of these projects I made having a good time was "Meaningless Adventure" (future post about this project with a prototype that’s been cooking). A cartoon project I thought was meaningless (therefore, the title hehe), caught the attention of several studios. This led to opportunities with different companies, including Roll7, where I created the art for OlliOlli World*.

To share something money related for artists, before this project got attention I was looking under the rocks for freelance jobs and I was trying to get 50-100€ per day, I had even no idea about how to think about what to charge. When this project brought me opportunities and some good people approached, my rate changed to 250-350€ per day. Just a tip, ask people around xd

3. Pursuing New Opportunities

Three years later, I left my full-time job at Roll7 to seek new challenges. I continued working on my own projects and freelancing for a few months until Yuga Labs offered me a position as Art Director. After some time in the company, I realised it wasn’t the right fit for me and decided to focus again on my own projects.

It wasn’t an easy decision, again, since it involved saying bye to stability.

But my goal has always been → getting enough savings so I got a parachute for some time and prioritise my artistic vision, this way I can say no. And shit, it is so important to say no sometimes.

Do your own projects, work in your own vision, try stuff. That’s the path to be an artist in my view and it’s what I pursue.

I’m not suggesting everyone should leave their job without a backup plan. Each person’s situation is unique. However, for me, taking these risks made sense and led to incredible opportunities. I've always planned my goals and worked towards them diligently. Reality strikes and things happen in different ways, but you shhhhould have a plan.

Think about what you want, plan what’s your goal and keep moving towards it. Daily small steps are better than rushing a day here and there. Stay consistent to build something cool (build something cool or drawing stupid cartoons lol).

So now it’s been almost a year since I left my last full-time job, and I´m starting a new adventure after a long process. Sneak peak on what´s happening now in the next newsletter <3

*In this video I explain my path more in depth.

title: Art Discipline .04
subtitle: A Confession: Public Speaking
excerpt: Does an artist need to know how to speak in public?
body:
Does an artist need to know how to speak in public?

Isn’t it a distraction from the actual work?

I’ve given a few talks by now — one in front of a live audience of about 700 people in the creative field. I’ve also conducted meetings and presentations for various companies I’ve worked with in different roles.

One might assume that with practice, my journey in public speaking is complete, problem solved. Bye.

Well… one might assume:

(Animation loading…)

I’m very scared of public speaking and still, I say yes to every public speaking opportunity I get, dumb dumb.

Recently, I attended an event to present Megalith, the project Lizz Lunney and I are co-developing. Megalith follows the adventure of two best friends traveling through the fantastical Megalith Islands. More about this project in future updates.

As usual, I prepared meticulously. I wrote the presentation, polished it, showed it to my partner, revised it again, practiced, polished—repeating this process through many iterations to keep it as controlled as possible. Boring the shit out of my partner with the practice.

But there’s something that’s hard to replicate in practice: standing in front of a live audience. Getting them to sleep. Still, I was confident—I’ve spoken in front of large groups before, and I’m a professional in the entertainment industry, right??

I arrived at the event, alone, and quickly realized that I’m not great at networking. It seemed like everyone else knew each other. So, I stuck to watching other presentations and wandering around.

I knew Megalith was strong — the narrative and the art were solid.

Yet, I found myself locked in ego battles throughout the event. At times, I thought, “I can do this better than the people in front of me.” Other times, the opposite: “I suck, they’re way ahead of me.” I struggled between these extremes. Normally, I stay grounded—I know my work, and I’m confident in what I’ve done, no comparisons. But in a setting like this in an event, insecurity creeps in, and the internal battles begin.

Then, the day arrived. I went up to the stage, trying to appear cool and collected, like someone with years of experience who’s got everything under control. lmao.

But I felt like a balloon, puffed up with air. The moment I stepped on stage, it deflated. An old, insecure part of me resurfaced, and I no longer felt like the seasoned artist I’ve tried to become. Instead, I was the same kid from years ago, unsure of myself, in an event where I didn’t know anyone — and no one knew me.

Then I looked at the screen, saw a page from Megalith, and realized: it was okay. The work was good. The story was strong. It wasn’t about me — it was about the story we wanted to tell.

Later, when I watched a recording of my presentation, I realized something surprising: I didn’t look panicked.

The conclusion, still scared as f*ck of speaking in public. It is a necessary evil. Work on your projects and less talking.
